# FULL degree-sequence split, one line per sub-cube.  Second opinion for
# Written by `iota_sym --checkpoint`; a row is appended the moment a
# sub-cube lands, so a reclaimed container loses only what was in flight.
# Resume with the same --checkpoint: UNSAT/SAT rows are skipped, UNKNOWN
# rows are re-run, because UNKNOWN is a budget and not a verdict.
# all_points_used = FALSE, so THE CUBE IS UNSAT ONLY WHEN ALL 1949
# SUB-CUBES ARE UNSAT.  This is NOT the same cover as
# docs/ladder/iota4_11.deg13.tsv, which holds 1939 -- that file was
# written through tools/rung.sh, which passes --ladder and so asks for a
# family on EXACTLY eleven points.  This run was launched from the binary
# without --ladder, so it asks for one on AT MOST eleven points: a
# strictly larger cover, 1939 of it shared and ten more carrying a
# degree-zero point.  UNSAT on all 1949 implies UNSAT on all 1939, so
# this is a sound second opinion and a slightly stronger one; the ten
# extras are redundant, being refuted already by iota(4,10) = 27 < 32.
# Do not merge rows between the two files.  See roadmap 52.1.
# THE SECONDS COLUMN IS WALL TIME UNDER CONTENTION and is not comparable
# with the cadical rows in iota4_11.deg13.tsv.  This ran on a 4-core
# session container alongside `cargo test --release` and `make verify`,
# and rows recording 664-820 s against a 600 s solver budget are the
# measure of that, not of the sub-cube.  Same caveat as roadmap 40.2.
# Why the full split and not the prefix-3 split that roadmap 50.3 asked
# for: the prefix-3 split of this cube is 27 sub-cubes, and the four ever
# attempted (under cadical, iota4_11.deg13.p3.tsv) all burned 2400 s
# without landing.  Those four are the first four in lexicographically
# descending enumeration order, covering 553, 325, 180 and 94 full
# sub-cubes -- 1152 of 1939, three fifths of the cube in four pieces.  At
# the 136-491 s a full sub-cube costs, the largest is ~10^5 s of search,
# so a 7200 s budget banks nothing.  The full split is what
# iota4_11.deg13.tsv calls the working granularity.  See roadmap 52.2.
# TWO PASSES, AND THE ROW COUNT IS NOT THE CUBE COUNT.  A 600 s pass ran
# first and banked 3 UNSAT of 20 attempted; an 1800 s pass then resumed
# against this same file, which skipped those 3 and re-ran the 17 UNKNOWN
# ones -- "checkpoint: 3 of 1949 cubes already decided".  The 600 s cap
# was too small for this solver: cryptominisat5 landed 1 of the 8
# sub-cubes it shares with cadical's pass, where cadical landed 5, so
# 600 s here is about a 200 s cadical-equivalent.
# `append_checkpoint` appends unconditionally and never dedups, so a
# re-run leaves the old UNKNOWN row in place beside the new one.  Rows are
# therefore >= cubes attempted, and a label may appear more than once.
# Only UNSAT/SAT rows are load-bearing, and those are written once; to
# count progress, count DISTINCT labels with an UNSAT verdict.
# WHAT THE 1800 s PASS BOUGHT, measured.  Its UNSAT rows land between
# 740.5 s and 1588.7 s -- all above the 600 s cap that had left them
# UNKNOWN, all under 1800 s.  So 600 s was cutting off sub-cubes this
# solver can decide, and the first pass's budget was largely wasted on
# them.  Two sub-cubes are still UNKNOWN at 1800 s, and the largest UNSAT
# used 88% of that budget, so a third pass at a larger cap would likely
# still gain -- it is not yet at the point of diminishing returns.
# STANDING, 21 distinct UNSAT of 42 labels attempted, 0 SAT.
# EVERY SUB-CUBE CADICAL EVER RECORDED FOR THIS CUBE IS NOW DECIDED, AND
# THE TWO SOLVERS AGREE ON ALL OF THEM.  cadical's pass attempted
# fourteen and landed five, leaving nine UNKNOWN at its 600 s cap.
# cryptominisat5 is UNSAT on all fourteen -- the five it confirms, and
# all nine cadical could not decide:
# So the portion of cube 13 that any solver has examined is now fully
# decided and fully agreed.  Seven further sub-cubes are decided beyond

# removes is the possibility that cadical's nine UNKNOWNs were hiding a
# SAT: they were not, and a SAT among them would have contradicted that

# STANDING: 91 UNSAT, 6 UNKNOWN, 0 SAT over 97 labels -- 91 of 1949, so
# 4.7% of the cube, and the rung's bound is untouched.  The rule's
# twelve-attempt window reads 0.82 UNSAT/h, down from 1.18 and 1.74 but
# still well clear of zero and flat across the last two batches, so the
# window reads 0.36; it is not the window the rule uses, for the reason
# recorded below -- it under-read the cap twice.
# THE STRAGGLERS, AND A SIXTH THAT IS NEW IN KIND.  Five labels have now
# stalled three or four times each at this cap, and every one of them
# stalled on its first attempt.  It is the first 5-family sub-cube this
# solver has failed to decide, against thirteen it decided, and it is
# the second thing in two batches to say the 5-family is not the cheap
# one this file briefly read it as.
# COST BY LEADING 13s, AND A READING THIS HEADER IS DECLINING TO MAKE:
# THE DECLINED READING WAS THE RIGHT CALL, AND TWO ROWS KILLED IT.  Last
# batch the 5-family read median 3653 s on eleven points, below both the
# 6- and 7-families, which on its face put a peak at six leading 13s.
# This header refused to claim it on the ground that eleven points is the
# opening of a family and every family opens cheap.  The next two points
# came in at 7412.9 s and 7838.0 s:
#     n = 11   median 3653     "peak at six" looked available
#     n = 12   median 4875     a third of the way to the 6-family
#     n = 14   median 5929     still level; the move was not a blip
# So the apparent peak was an artefact of a family's opening, exactly as
# the refusal said it might be.  This is the second time in this file
# that a reading taken at a family's opening has been overturned by its
# continuation -- the first was the 6-family's own 4806 s at n = 7,
# refuted at n = 25.  The rule that survives both: NEVER READ A MEDIAN
# BEFORE THE FAMILY IS PAST ITS OPENING, and the opening is longer than
# it looks.  n = 13 is still not past it; what is measured is that the
# 5-family is at least as expensive as the 6-family, not that it is
# AND EVERY FAMILY OPENS CHEAP.  The 5-family's first two sub-cubes cost
# 936 s and 3108 s, against a 6-family median of 6136 s.  Same pattern as
# the 6-family's 731 s opener and the 7-family's 756 s.  A cheap row
# right after an expensive one usually means the enumeration has crossed
# into a new family, not that the frontier has eased -- which is why the
# median per family is the thing to read, and never a single row.
# TWO THINGS MAKE A SUB-CUBE CHEAP, AND THE RANKING BETWEEN THEM HAS
# ALREADY FLIPPED ONCE.  Correlation of UNSAT cost against candidate
# predictors, recomputed over all 91 decided sub-cubes, with the reading
#     distinct values    r = +0.69     r = +0.63   <- best now
# THE HEADER'S OWN WARNING CAME TRUE ON ITS OWN DATA.  At n = 67 this
# table called leading 13s "the best single predictor" and then said "do
# not over-fit this".  Twenty-four sub-cubes later leading 13s has fallen
# from -0.75 to -0.62 and distinct values has passed it.  Nothing about
# the cube changed; the sample did.  Treat every r in this table as a
# statement about the 89 sub-cubes measured, not about the cube.
# The structural reading is unchanged and is what survives the flip: the
# leading-13s model alone cannot explain three sub-cubes that all open
# with six 13s and cost 1111 s, 1871 s and 10866 s.  Their minimum
# degrees are 2, 6 and 8.  Both effects are the same structural fact from
# opposite ends: a run of MAXIMAL degrees constrains the family, and so
# does a point of NEAR-ZERO degree, because it is a point almost nothing
# uses.  The expensive sub-cubes are the ones that are flat in the
# middle -- no long run of 13s and no nearly-unused point.  "Distinct
# values" is a third measure of the same flatness, which is why it moves
# Do not over-fit this: n = 91, and no family below five leading 13s is
# measured, which is where the remaining ~1860 sub-cubes are.
# THE RULE HELD, AND NEEDED A WINDOW.  Last batch the 10800 s cap read
# 0.21 UNSAT per wall-hour over its last eight attempts -- three stalls
# in four, which looks exactly like the wall that ended the 600 s and
# 5400 s caps.  The rule said hold, because 0.21 is not zero.  It was
# right: the next batch went three for four and the rate recovered.
#     10800 s cap, whole life   11 UNSAT / 16 attempts   1.18 UNSAT/h
# So an eight-attempt window is too noisy to trigger a raise -- batches
# are four wide and a single bad one halves it.  **Read the rate over at
# least twelve attempts.**  The 5400 s cap's terminal reading was zero
# over sixteen, which is why that one was real.
# WHAT THE 10800 s CAP HAS BOUGHT.  Seven sub-cubes decided above 5400 s,
# so unreachable at the previous cap, at 6136, 6397, 6468, 6490, 6956,
# 7179 and 8626 s.  Four of those were the ones this header had named as
# "confirmed beyond 5400 s" after stalling three times each -- and it was
# wrong about what they needed, saying "a session with more cores".  They
# needed 6500 s on the same four threads.  Stalling repeatedly at a cap
# establishes that the cap is too small and nothing else: not that the
# instance is out of reach, and not which resource it is short of.
# THE PRICE OF THE RAISE, MEASURED.  Seven UNSAT for 97188 core-s = 6.75 h
# wall on four threads = 1.04 UNSAT per wall-hour, against 2.15/h that the
# 5400 s cap managed at its best and 0.00/h once it stopped converting.
# So raising halves the peak rate and beats the terminal one, which is
# exactly what the rule below predicts and why it is conditional.
# WHEN TO RAISE THE CAP, AND WHY THIS HEADER SAID IT WRONG TWICE.
# The quantity is UNSAT BANKED PER WALL-HOUR, and it is a comparison
# against the CURRENT cap's rate -- which is not constant, so the answer
# changes as the run walks deeper.  Both of this header's earlier
# instructions were stated flatly and were conditional:
#   "raising by threes has worked twice, the next step is 16200 s"
#       -- wrong while 5400 s was still converting at 2.15 UNSAT/h,
#          because 16200 s needs more than 9.7 of four attempts to land
#          to beat that, and there are four.
#       -- wrong once 5400 s stopped converting.  Conversion over the
#          last 24, 16 and 8 labels attempted was 54%, 38%, 0%.  The
#          last eight cost 43504 core-s (3.02 h wall on four threads)
#          and banked NOTHING, so the current rate is 0.00 UNSAT/h and
#          any nonzero conversion at a larger cap beats it.
# The rule, stated so it does not need correcting a third time:
# **raise when the current cap's UNSAT-per-wall-hour has fallen to
# roughly zero, and not before.**  Raising early costs throughput;
# raising late costs nothing but the batch that measured it.
# RAISED TO 10800 s on that basis -- a doubling rather than the 3x used
# twice before, because it gives feedback in half the time and nothing
# here says a larger step converts more.  It is a bet: the eight
# sub-cubes that stalled at 5400 s may need 6000 s or 60000, and this
# file does not know which.  The known quantity is that 5400 s now
# COST OF THE DECIDED SUB-CUBES, in order of first attempt, per eight:
# The largest UNSAT anywhere in this file is 5313 s of a 5400 s budget;
# WHAT ACTUALLY PREDICTS A SUB-CUBE'S COST: THE NUMBER OF LEADING 13s.
# Not its position in the enumeration, which was this header's earlier
# model and only correlates.  Median UNSAT time of the decided sub-cubes,
# grouped by how many maximal degrees the sequence opens with:
# The cost rises about six-fold from nine leading 13s to seven and then
# looks flat, though the 6-family has only five points and its cheapest
# is 1111 s, so the flattening is not established.  The mechanism is the
# one already in this header: a run of maximal degrees is a strong
# constraint, and removing one makes the sub-cube freer and harder to
# THIS EXPLAINS THE SCATTER.  Sub-cubes are enumerated lexicographically
# descending, so the families come in blocks and each new block RESETS to
# its own cheap end -- the 1111 s row is the first of the 6-family, not a
# fluke deep in the 7-family.  So "position in the enumeration" mispredicts
# exactly at the block boundaries.  Group by leading 13s and read the
# median; do not read a trend off single rows, and do not treat a cheap
# row after an expensive one as the frontier easing.
# WHAT THIS SAYS ABOUT THE REMAINING ~1890.  They lie in families with
# progressively fewer leading 13s, which on this evidence are at least as
# expensive as the 7- and 6-families and possibly worse.  Nothing here
# measures a family below six, and roadmap 48.2's rule applies: every
# extrapolation attempted on this ladder has been wrong, this session's
# THE ENUMERATION RUNS EASY TO HARD, AND AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS
# HEADER HAD IT BACKWARDS.  It said lexicographically descending order
# puts "the MOST extreme, and so the hardest" sub-cubes first, and
# concluded the mean would fall over the remaining 1949.  Measured, in
# blocks of eight attempts in first-seen order:
#     attempts   stalled at the 1800 s cap   mean wall
# Extreme is not the same as hard: a sequence with the degree mass
# concentrated on a few points is MORE constrained and so easier to
# refute, and those are exactly the ones lex-descending order takes
# first.  The first eight are the same eight the 600 s pass could land.
# THE 1800 s BUDGET IS EXHAUSTED AS A PRODUCER OF VERDICTS.  The last
# sixteen attempts stalled sixteen times; every UNSAT this file holds
# landed between 128.3 s and 1588.7 s, and nothing has landed since.
# Continuing at 1800 s banks nothing while still costing 1810 s a
# sub-cube, which is the same shape of loss iota4_11.deg13.p3.tsv
# records under "TOO COARSE, and the budget is the result".  The budget
# was raised rather than the run continued; see the command above.
